discoveries: THE GATE NAMES A KEY THAT DOES NOT EXIST, AND I WROTE THE GATE'S NAME INTO THE REGISTRY. Release Gate B reports `missing_scene_path`, and the artifact audit's output field is spelled `scene_path` -- but the registry INPUT key the audit actually reads is `scene` (spine_map_workbench.py:275, `value.get("scene", "")`). Corpus-wide the split is 2686 entries using `scene` against 15 using `scene_path`. Told to fill in a missing scene path, I copied the name off the gate's own report, wrote `"scene_path": "res://..."` into dark_spot.json, and re-ran the audit: still 1. The JSON stayed valid, the file parsed, the entry looked complete to any human reading it, and NOTHING in the chain objected -- no schema check, no linter, no gate. The fix was a one-word rename to `scene`, after which the count went to 0. The general shape: when a report's field name and the data's field name differ, the report teaches the wrong name to whoever acts on it, and the wrong name fails silently because JSON has no unknown-key error.

THE 14 `scene_path` ENTRIES ARE A DORMANT VERSION OF THE SAME TRAP. commons_artifacts.json (6), physics_simulation.json (7) and procgen_extra.json (1) carry BOTH keys, and in all 14 the two values are byte-identical, so nothing is wrong today. But `scene` is the only one read; if any of those 14 is ever updated by editing the visible-looking `scene_path`, the artifact keeps loading the stale scene and every gate stays green. Not repaired -- 14 surgical edits across three tab-indented registries to delete a no-op is a worse risk than the trap. Recorded so the next hand knows which key is live.
